study.design: case-control study (1:7) within an ICU cohort, single centre
study.environment: ICU (13 beds) of a tertiary university hospital
study.source_details: C1: blood cultures from critically ill ICU patients with candidaemia
study.identification_method: Germ tube test; API 20C AUX or Vitek 2 YST card
study.standard_document: EUCAST breakpoint tables for antifungal agents
study.azole_exposure: Antifungal prophylaxis/treatment common in the ICU (azoles given to 36.9% of controls and 21.2% of non-albicans cases; fluconazole most used); not reported specifically for the C. tropicalis cases
study.comments: Species-specific susceptibility tables are not given; counts for C. tropicalis are inferred because the text lists the species of every non-susceptible/resistant isolate (none were C. tropicalis) and states all isolates were susceptible to amphotericin B. It is assumed all 4 isolates were tested with every agent. EUCAST has no caspofungin breakpoints and micafungin breakpoints for C. tropicalis were 'insufficient evidence', so only n_R = 0 is recorded for these.

study.comments: Counts calculated from percentages and n per agent (Tables 2–3). The abstract gives fluconazole R 36.2% as '21/58' and voriconazole R 34.8% as '20/58', inconsistent with n = 290 in Table 2. Different AST kits across hospitals (acknowledged limitation). Year-specific denominators for resistance trends are only shown graphically (Figure 2).

clade4.note: No genotyping performed; discussion cites ERG11, UPC2, MDR1 and CDR1 mechanisms from the literature but no clade or cluster.

dynamics.description: C. tropicalis fluconazole resistance peaked in 2021 at 55.5% (p < 0.01) and declined over 2022–2023 (p < 0.05); overall 36.2%. Annual values otherwise only in Figure 2.
C. tropicalis voriconazole resistance peaked in 2021 at 50.8% (p < 0.01) and declined over 2022–2023 (p < 0.05); overall 34.8%.
C. tropicalis bloodstream isolates per year: 2019 46/356, 2020 45/341, 2021 70/523, 2022 22/227, 2023 107/587 (all fungal BSI isolates as denominator).

study.design: cross-sectional (health facility-based) with WGS of 3 isolates and an animal pathogenicity experiment
study.region_city: Abakaliki, Ebonyi State (Alex Ekwueme Federal University Teaching Hospital; St Patrick's Mile Four Hospital)
study.environment: HIV clinics of a public teaching hospital (urban) and a private/missionary hospital (rural)
study.source_details: C1: oral swabs from 514 people living with HIV/AIDS (Candida in 195)
study.population: people living with HIV/AIDS on HAART (adults and minors)
study.standard_document: CLSI M100-S20 (bacterial performance standard, as cited)
study.breakpoint_type: clinical CBP (as cited; not a yeast standard)
study.azole_exposure: None recent: individuals on antifungal drugs, immunosuppressants or antibiotics in the previous 6 months were excluded
study.comments: Serious methodological concerns: disc diffusion interpreted with a bacterial CLSI standard (M100-S20), which has no yeast azole breakpoints; species identified only on chromogenic agar; implausible 99.5% azole resistance. WGS/MLST was done only on C. glabrata, C. albicans and C. krusei (labels swapped between text and Table 1) using bacterial housekeeping genes (argS, gyrB, ileS, nuoC, ppsA, recA, rpoB, rpoD) and bacterial virulence genes; no C. tropicalis was sequenced. Collection period not stated (ethics approval 2023). Counts calculated from %.

resistance.note: Calculated from % (33.3% resistant); S/I split not reported.

clade4.note: The 'ST15' clonal lineage reported refers to C. albicans, C. glabrata and C. krusei typed with bacterial housekeeping genes; no C. tropicalis typing.
